title: Two Pointers
summary: Walk two indices through the data instead of one, using a property of the data (usually sortedness) to decide which one to move — replacing a nested loop with a single pass.

analogy.beginner: You and a friend stand at opposite ends of a shelf of books arranged by price, trying to find two books that together cost exactly ₹500. You look at the cheapest and the most expensive. Too expensive together? Your friend moves to a cheaper book. Too cheap? You move up. Neither of you ever walks backwards, so between you the shelf is crossed only once — instead of comparing every book with every other book.
analogy.interview: Maintain two indices over a sequence and derive a rule, from an ordering or monotonicity property, that lets each comparison eliminate a whole class of candidate pairs. Because each pointer moves monotonically in one direction, the total movement is O(n).

intuition:
The brute force for pair problems is 'every i with every j' — O(n²). Two pointers is what you get when the data gives you enough information to rule out many pairs from a single comparison.

On a **sorted** array with pointers at both ends: if `a[left] + a[right]` is too large, then `a[right]` paired with *anything* from left onwards is also too large, because everything from left onwards is ≥ a[left]. So moving `right` inwards discards an entire column of the comparison table in one step. That is where the factor of n goes.

There are three shapes, and recognising which one you need is the actual skill:

1. **Opposite ends** (converging) — sorted input, pair/triplet sums, palindromes, container problems.
2. **Same direction** (fast and slow) — deduplication in place, removing elements, partitioning. One pointer reads, one writes.
3. **Two sequences** — merging sorted arrays, checking subsequences, intersecting sorted lists.

The sliding window is a special case of shape 2 where the region between the pointers is the thing you care about.

problemFirst.motivatingProblem: Given a **sorted** array and a target, find two numbers that add up to the target. Return their indices.

code: for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {
bruteForce.whySlow: It throws away the most useful fact we have: the array is sorted. It will happily compare 1 + 2 when the target is 500 and the array ends in 499.

problemFirst.observation: Start at the two extremes. Their sum is the largest possible involving the smallest element, and the smallest possible involving the largest element. If that sum is too big, the *largest* element cannot participate in any valid pair at all — every other partner is even smaller. So discard it entirely.
problemFirst.leap: Each comparison eliminates one whole element from consideration, so at most n comparisons are needed. O(n) after an O(n log n) sort — or O(n) outright if the input is already sorted.
optimizedSketch: if (sum == target) return new int[]{left, right};
if (sum < target) left++;      // need more: only bigger values can help
else                right--;   // need less: only smaller values can help

howItWorks: **Opposite ends**: `left = 0`, `right = n-1`; loop while `left < right`; compare and move the pointer that can improve the situation.

**Same direction (read/write)**: `slow` marks where the next kept element goes, `fast` scans ahead. Write only when `fast` finds something worth keeping. This is how in-place removal works in O(1) space.
**Two sequences**: one index per array, advance whichever is behind. This is the merge step of merge sort.
**The decision rule is the whole pattern.** Justify in one sentence why moving that pointer cannot skip a valid answer — if you cannot, two pointers is the wrong tool.
**Sorting first is allowed** when the problem asks for values rather than original indices. Say so explicitly: it costs O(n log n) but unlocks O(n) scanning.

signals: The array is **sorted**, or you are allowed to sort it
You are looking for a **pair or triplet** satisfying a condition
Palindrome checking — compare inwards from both ends
In-place modification with O(1) extra space: remove duplicates, move zeroes, partition
Merging or comparing two sorted sequences
The brute force is two nested loops over the same array
antiSignals: The array is unsorted and you must return original indices — sorting destroys them, so use a HashMap
The answer depends on a contiguous range's aggregate — that is a sliding window
There is no ordering or monotonic property to exploit; nothing justifies the pointer move

implementations.explanation: The converging template. The comment on each branch is the justification — always be able to say why the discarded element can never be part of an answer.
code: /** Two sum on a SORTED array. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
public static int[] twoSumSorted(int[] nums, int target) {
left++;    // nums[left] is too small to pair with ANY remaining value
right--;   // nums[right] is too large to pair with ANY remaining value

implementations.label: Optimized
implementations.explanation: Three Sum is the classic application: sort, fix one element, and two-point the remainder. It is O(n²) rather than O(n³), and the duplicate-skipping is the part candidates usually miss.
code: /** All unique triplets summing to zero. O(n log n + n^2) = O(n^2). */
if (nums[i] > 0) break;                       // sorted: no way back to zero
if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue; // skip duplicate anchors

complexity.time: O(n) for a single two-pointer pass; O(n log n) if you must sort first; O(n²) for Three Sum (an anchor loop wrapping a two-pointer pass)
complexity.space: O(1) — this is the pattern's other selling point. Unlike the HashMap approach to pair problems, it allocates nothing.
complexity.why: Each comparison moves exactly one pointer, and pointers only move inwards (or only forwards), so the total number of iterations is bounded by n. The O(1) space matters in interviews: if you are asked for two sum on a sorted array, the map solution is O(n) space and the two-pointer solution is O(1), so the pointers win. On unsorted input where original indices matter, that reverses — the map is the right answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `left <= right` in the converging loop
commonMistakes.fix: That lets an element pair with itself. For distinct pairs, `left < right`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying opposite-end pointers to an unsorted array
commonMistakes.fix: The pointer-move rule is justified only by ordering. Without it, moving `left` can skip the answer. Sort first, or use a HashMap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sorting when the problem needs original indices
commonMistakes.fix: Sorting destroys them. Either store (value, index) pairs, or use a HashMap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to skip duplicates in Three Sum
commonMistakes.fix: You emit the same triplet repeatedly. Skip equal anchors, and skip equal values after recording a hit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Moving both pointers when the sum matches
commonMistakes.fix: Fine for two sum, but in Three Sum you must also skip duplicates or you loop on the same values.

realWorldUses: Merging sorted result sets — the merge step of merge sort, and how databases combine sorted index scans.
Streaming joins over two sorted inputs, without loading either into memory.
In-place compaction: garbage collectors and log compaction use read/write pointers to squeeze out dead entries.
Diff algorithms walk two sequences with independent indices.
interviewNotes: Ask whether the input is sorted before you design anything. If yes, two pointers or binary search is almost always intended.
Emphasise O(1) space — it is the standard follow-up after you give the HashMap solution.
Justify each pointer move out loud: 'nums[right] is too large to pair with anything remaining, so it can be discarded'. That sentence is the proof of correctness.

quiz.question: Why can't you use opposite-end two pointers on an unsorted array for two sum?
options: Without ordering there is no justification that moving a pointer cannot skip a valid pair
Unsorted arrays cannot be indexed from both ends
quiz.explanation: The correctness argument is 'everything to the right is larger, so this element cannot help'. Remove sortedness and that reasoning evaporates; a valid pair could sit on either side of wherever you move.

quiz.question: 'Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length, using O(1) extra space.' Which shape?
quiz.explanation: `fast` reads every element; `slow` marks where the next kept element belongs. Writing only on a change compacts the array in place with no extra allocation.

quiz.question: What is the complexity of Three Sum using sort + two pointers?
quiz.explanation: An O(n) two-pointer scan inside an O(n) anchor loop gives O(n²); the O(n log n) sort is dominated by it. Brute force over all triplets would be O(n³).

quiz.question: For two sum on an *unsorted* array where you must return the original indices, what is the best approach?
options: HashMap of value → index, one pass
quiz.explanation: Sorting would destroy the indices. A HashMap gives O(n) time at the cost of O(n) space — the correct trade when identity, not just value, matters.
